paragraphs: A targeted adversarial attack changes an image so that a classifier favors a chosen label. This paper studies a more demanding version: making several chosen labels occupy the highest positions in a specified order. It also asks how to calculate the image changes needed to produce that ranking.

The authors connect these changes to the adversarial Jacobian, which describes how image changes affect output scores under the ranking constraints. Its right singular vectors provide mutually orthogonal directions in image space. The paper shows that ordered attacks can be learned by repeatedly optimizing combinations of these directions. RisingAttacK uses sequential quadratic programming to exploit this structure.

The evaluation combines attack success with several measures of perturbation size, making both effectiveness and image modification part of the assessment. Across the tested ImageNet-1k rankings and four convolutional and transformer models, RisingAttacK consistently outperforms QuadAttacK. The contribution is both a structural account of how these perturbations can be constructed and an attack algorithm built around that account.
icml-2025-adversarial-perturbations-are-.tldr: RisingAttacK builds ordered adversarial attacks by optimizing combinations of informative image-space directions derived from a constrained Jacobian.

paragraphs: This paper examines logical reasoning through Boolean satisfiability: deciding whether truth values can be assigned so that a logical formula is satisfied. The authors separate two questions that are easy to conflate: whether a decoder-only Transformer can represent a solving procedure, and whether training can teach it to follow one.

For the first question, they construct a Transformer that decides 3-SAT using deduction and backtracking expressed through chain-of-thought. The proof uses a non-uniform model of computation, so its conclusion carries that qualification. They also implement the construction in PyTorch using their PARAT tool to demonstrate correctness empirically and investigate the model's behavior.

For the learning question, they train models on algorithmic reasoning traces generated from the construction. These models generalize strongly to out-of-distribution examples at problem sizes represented during training, but their ability to generalize to longer problems is limited. The findings therefore distinguish successful learning within familiar sizes from length generalization, while connecting the observed behavior to the theoretical construction.
icml-2025-can-transformers-reason-logica.tldr: A constructive proof and training experiments show how Transformers can solve SAT, while revealing limited generalization to longer problems.

paragraphs: Unrestricted adversarial examples can change an image more extensively than attacks constrained by a fixed perturbation budget. The challenge is to create images that remain natural while misleading a neural network. This paper addresses a further difficulty: existing diffusion-based approaches are often designed around particular attack conditions, which restricts their flexibility.

DiffAdvMAP frames image generation as sampling from a posterior distribution of adversarial examples. It approximates that distribution using the real-image prior learned by a diffusion model. An adversarial constraint promotes attack effectiveness, while a reconstruction constraint allows the framework to be adapted to different attack scenarios. These components connect natural appearance, adversarial behavior, and scenario-specific requirements within one formulation.

Experiments on ImageNet report a better balance of image quality, flexibility, and transferability than the baseline unrestricted attacks. The authors also report strong attack ability and robustness against defenses. The stated result concerns the combined trade-off: the framework aims to produce convincing images while remaining useful across attack conditions, rather than treating visual quality as the sole objective.
icml-2025-diffadvmap-flexible-diffusion-.tldr: DiffAdvMAP combines diffusion priors with attack and reconstruction constraints to generate natural adversarial images across different attack scenarios.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization problems whose objective is the difference of two submodular functions. Earlier work focused on set functions; the authors extend the treatment to discrete and continuous domains. They show that every function on a discrete domain, and every smooth function on a continuous domain, admits such a representation.

That broad representation result matters because it connects many possible objectives to a common optimization framework. For discrete domains, the authors establish an equivalence with minimizing the difference of two convex functions. They then introduce a variant of the Difference of Convex Algorithm and apply it to the resulting optimization problem, obtaining theoretical guarantees comparable to those available for set functions.

The algorithm can also be used on continuous domains after discretization. Experiments in integer compressive sensing and integer least squares show better performance than the evaluated baselines. Together, the results extend both the mathematical scope and the algorithmic usefulness of this decomposition, with the reported practical gains demonstrated on those two integer optimization applications.
icml-2025-discrete-and-continuous-differ.tldr: The paper extends difference-of-submodular optimization beyond set functions and develops an algorithm with theoretical guarantees and gains on two integer optimization tasks.

paragraphs: Researchers use variational autoencoders to represent single-cell measurements in a compact latent space and interpolate between cellular states. A straight line in that space is convenient, but it need not follow a geodesic on the decoded data manifold. Consequently, downstream methods that assume Euclidean geometry may rely on a property the representation never learned.

FlatVI addresses this mismatch during training. It regularizes the latent manifold of variational autoencoders with discrete likelihoods toward Euclidean geometry, specifically for single-cell count data. The aim is to make straight latent paths approximate geodesic interpolations after decoding. This encourages a geometric relationship between the representation and the cellular data it generates.

Synthetic-data experiments support the approach's theoretical basis, while experiments with time-resolved single-cell RNA sequencing show improved trajectory reconstruction and manifold interpolation. The significance is practical: methods built around straight latent movements become more compatible with the trained representation. The stated goal is an approximation encouraged by regularization, rather than a claim that every decoded straight line becomes an exact geodesic.
icml-2025-enforcing-latent-euclidean-geo.tldr: FlatVI trains single-cell variational autoencoders so that straight latent paths better approximate geodesic paths in decoded cellular data.

paragraphs: Many datasets contain nested groups, making it useful to recover relationships at several levels of detail. This paper examines deep models designed specifically for hierarchical clustering and finds substantial scalability and performance limitations on realistic datasets. Those findings motivate a lighter approach that reuses information already produced by pretrained models.

The proposed method builds a hierarchy from a pretrained, non-hierarchical clustering model that outputs logits, its numerical scores before conversion into probabilities. It requires no fine-tuning and is broadly applicable to clustering models meeting that output requirement. This makes the hierarchy-building step usable with existing trained models, rather than requiring a specialized hierarchical architecture.

The authors report that their method outperforms the specialized deep hierarchical clustering models they evaluate, with advantages in efficiency and scalability as well as performance. They also apply it to a pretrained ImageNet classifier and recover meaningful hierarchies in a supervised setting. That extension shows that useful hierarchical information can be extracted from outputs learned for an ordinary classification task.
icml-2025-from-logits-to-hierarchies-hie.tldr: A lightweight method extracts hierarchies from pretrained models' logits without fine-tuning and outperforms evaluated specialized hierarchical clustering models.

paragraphs: Generating spatially structured graphs often involves learning to reverse a process that gradually adds noise. Existing approaches use graph networks whose architecture stays the same across noise levels. This paper argues that such a fixed architecture limits expressiveness because the information useful for generation changes with the amount of noise.

The authors introduce Noise-Conditioned Graph Networks, which adapt their architecture to the current noise level. Their theoretical and empirical analysis identifies two relevant patterns: noisier graphs need information from more distant neighbors, and they can be represented effectively at lower resolution. Dynamic Message Passing turns those findings into a model that changes both the reach and the resolution of its message passing.

Dynamic Message Passing consistently outperforms noise-independent architectures across the evaluated domains, including 3D point clouds, spatiotemporal transcriptomics, and images. The contribution connects architectural choices directly to the changing generation problem. Instead of treating every noise level as requiring the same information exchange, the network adjusts how broadly and at what detail it processes the graph.
icml-2025-geometric-generative-modeling-.tldr: Noise-conditioned graph networks improve geometric generation by adapting message-passing range and resolution to the current noise level.

paragraphs: Groups in a graph can be nested within larger groups, and a node can belong to more than one group. These hierarchical and overlapping patterns often occur together, but studying them separately leaves the combined structure difficult to evaluate. This paper develops an objective and an algorithm for clustering that captures both.

The authors introduce a cost function and justify it through several intuitive properties. They also develop an approximation algorithm with a constant-factor guarantee for the dual version of the problem. The algorithm recursively divides groups into two potentially overlapping parts, using local search to find those divisions. That framework also supports a faster variant intended for large graphs.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the accelerated algorithm significantly outperforms all evaluated baselines in effectiveness and scalability. The work therefore contributes both a way to judge hierarchical overlapping clusterings and a practical way to produce them. The theoretical approximation statement applies specifically to the dual formulation, while the scalability findings come from the experimental evaluation.
icml-2025-hierarchical-overlapping-clust.tldr: The paper introduces an objective and scalable algorithm for graph clusters that are both nested and overlapping.

paragraphs: LiDAR provides sparse 3D measurements, which can make small or distant objects difficult to recognize. Camera images offer dense texture information that can help, but combining the sensors creates its own problems. This paper focuses on maintaining alignment during data augmentation and predicting panoptic segmentation results directly through a decoder.

Image-Assists-LiDAR, or IAL, coordinates several components around those goals. PieAug synchronizes augmentation across the two modalities so that their inputs remain aligned. Geometric-guided Token Fusion combines image and LiDAR features into tokens for a transformer decoder. Prior-based Query Generation uses the complementary strengths of the sensors to initialize the decoder's queries and support accurate instance masks.

Together, these components address alignment, feature fusion, and prediction within one framework. IAL achieves state-of-the-art performance relative to previous multimodal 3D panoptic segmentation methods on two widely used benchmarks. The reported result supports the value of coordinating how the modalities interact throughout the system, including how they are augmented and how their information initializes the final predictions.
icml-2025-how-do-images-align-and-comple.tldr: IAL improves multimodal 3D panoptic segmentation through synchronized augmentation, geometry-guided feature fusion, and sensor-informed decoder queries.

paragraphs: GPU kernels are the computational routines behind machine learning workloads, and efficient implementations require considerable engineering expertise. KernelBench evaluates whether language models can automate that work. Its open-source framework contains 250 selected PyTorch workloads, grounding the evaluation in tasks where better generated code can translate into practical speed improvements.

The benchmark evaluates correctness and speed together. Its fast_p metric counts the percentage of generated kernels that are functionally correct and exceed a configurable speedup threshold over the baseline. Changing that threshold makes the performance requirement stricter or more permissive, so successful code generation cannot be reduced to producing runnable code alone.

Across the tested models and inference methods, frontier reasoning models perform best without refinement, but still reach the PyTorch baseline in fewer than 20% of cases. Iterative refinement using execution and profiling feedback can improve results. Nevertheless, the benchmark remains difficult, especially as the required speedup increases, exposing a substantial gap between generating code and reliably generating fast, correct GPU implementations.
icml-2025-kernelbench-can-llms-write-eff.tldr: KernelBench tests language models on 250 GPU workloads and finds that producing kernels that are both correct and fast remains challenging.

paragraphs: Transformers need positional information to represent the spatial arrangement of their inputs. Rotary Position Encoding supplies this through fixed rotations applied to queries and keys. The authors hypothesize that its restricted arrangement of two-dimensional rotations limits its usefulness for modalities with higher-dimensional structure, motivating a more flexible way to encode positions.

LieRE learns dense skew-symmetric matrices and maps them differentiably into higher-dimensional rotation matrices. The learned matrices belong to a Lie algebra, while the resulting rotations belong to a Lie group. This construction preserves a rotation-based formulation while expanding the positional relationships the model can represent. It encodes both relative and absolute position continuously.

Experiments on 2D and 3D vision tasks demonstrate the method's effectiveness and its ability to generalize to higher input resolutions while maintaining computational efficiency. These findings support learnable, richer rotations as a useful positional encoding design for the evaluated visual settings. The proposed restriction of conventional RoPE remains the motivating hypothesis, rather than a universal conclusion about every modality or task.
icml-2025-liere-lie-rotational-positiona.tldr: LieRE generalizes rotary positional encoding with learned higher-dimensional rotations, showing effectiveness and resolution generalization on 2D and 3D vision tasks.

paragraphs: A treatment can have different effects for people with different characteristics. Estimating those differences is only part of the task; researchers also want to know which measured variables matter for the variation. This paper develops a statistically rigorous way to assess global variable importance when estimating conditional average treatment effects.

The proposed algorithm, PermuCATE, builds on Conditional Permutation Importance. It evaluates variable importance for the treatment-effect estimation problem, helping characterize heterogeneity across the population. The authors compare it with Leave-One-Covariate-Out, an alternative importance method, using both finite-sample theoretical analysis and empirical studies. Their results show that PermuCATE has lower variance and provides a reliable importance measure.

Lower variance increases statistical power, making relevant differences easier to detect when the available sample is finite. Experiments on simulated and real datasets demonstrate the benefits, including settings with many correlated variables. The contribution is a more statistically effective assessment of which variables matter to treatment-effect heterogeneity, complementing the estimation of how treatment responses vary across individuals.
icml-2025-measuring-variable-importance-.tldr: PermuCATE measures variable importance in treatment-effect heterogeneity with lower variance and greater statistical power than Leave-One-Covariate-Out.

paragraphs: Neural combinatorial optimization uses learned policies to construct solutions to problems such as routing and scheduling. Reinforcement learning can teach these heuristics without expert demonstrations, but weak reward signals and enormous action spaces can make learning inefficient. This paper changes how the training process represents feedback about solution quality.

Preference Optimization converts numerical rewards into comparisons indicating which sampled solutions are better. Through a policy-based reparameterization of reward and statistical preference models, the authors formulate an entropy-regularized reinforcement learning objective that aligns the policy with those comparisons while avoiding intractable computations. Local search is incorporated into fine-tuning to produce high-quality preference pairs and help the policy escape local optima.

The method significantly outperforms existing reinforcement learning algorithms on the evaluated benchmarks, including traveling salesman, capacitated vehicle routing, and flexible flow shop problems. The reported benefits cover both convergence efficiency and solution quality. Its central contribution is to make relative solution quality a direct training signal, while using local search to improve the comparisons from which the policy learns.
icml-2025-preference-optimization-for-co.tldr: Preference Optimization trains combinatorial solvers from solution comparisons and incorporates local search into fine-tuning to improve convergence and solution quality.

paragraphs: Generative Flow Networks learn to generate diverse molecular structures using reward values as an unnormalized target distribution. Previous approaches often assemble molecules from predefined fragments, which restricts the structures they can explore. Atomic GFlowNets instead use individual atoms as building blocks, enabling more comprehensive exploration of drug-like chemical space.

The paper proposes pretraining with inexpensive molecular descriptors, including drug-likeliness, topological polar surface area, and synthetic accessibility scores. These proxy rewards teach the model to favor promising regions of chemical space without requiring the pretraining objective to be a particular final drug-design target. Goal-conditioned fine-tuning then adapts the pretrained model to optimize specific properties.

The authors pretrain on a subset of ZINC and evaluate against relevant baselines across a range of drug-design tasks, reporting evidence of the approach's effectiveness. The method combines greater building-block flexibility with reusable learning from inexpensive rewards. Its pharmacological guidance comes through proxy properties, followed by target-specific adaptation, rather than treating the initial descriptors as the complete design objective.
icml-2025-pretraining-generative-flow-ne.tldr: Atomic GFlowNets generate molecules atom by atom, using inexpensive proxy rewards for pretraining before adaptation to specific design goals.

paragraphs: Quantization reduces the numerical precision used to represent model weights and activations, potentially lowering language-model costs. QuEST studies training directly with compressed representations through quantization-aware training. The authors report an optimal operating point at four bits and stable convergence down to one-bit weights and activations, which are distinct findings.

QuEST improves both quantization and gradient estimation. Hadamard normalization and mean-squared-error-optimal fitting provide accurate, fast quantization of continuous weight and activation distributions. A trust gradient estimator explicitly targets the discrepancy between gradients computed from quantized states and the unknown full-precision gradient. Together, these changes address numerical representation and the reliability of the updates used during training.

Experiments with Llama-type architectures show stable scaling laws across hardware-supported precisions, and the approach can extend to sparse representations. GPU kernel support also demonstrates efficient execution of the resulting models. The one-bit result establishes stable training at very low precision; the abstract's separate four-bit optimality claim should not be read as establishing equal accuracy or optimality at every tested precision.
icml-2025-quest-stable-training-of-llms-.tldr: QuEST improves quantization and gradient estimation, reporting four-bit optimality and stable language-model training down to one-bit weights and activations.

paragraphs: Feature selection reduces the number of inputs a model uses, potentially improving efficiency and interpretability. Existing methods can require extensive tuning and retraining after features are selected. SAND introduces a selection layer that learns which inputs to retain during neural-network training, given a desired feature count k.

For each input, the layer mixes the original feature with Gaussian noise using a trainable gain. The gains are normalized so that their squared values sum to k. Weighted noise distortion and normalization induce a clustering effect: k gains move toward one, preserving their features, while the remaining gains move toward zero, replacing those inputs with noise.

The authors report competitive results on standard benchmarks and a new real-world dataset, often matching or exceeding existing methods. The approach avoids post-selection retraining and does not require changing the loss or redesigning the underlying network. Linear-regression analysis provides additional theoretical support. Its practical appeal lies in integrating the requested feature budget into training through a compact mechanism rather than a separate selection-and-retraining procedure.
icml-2025-sand-one-shot-feature-selectio.tldr: SAND selects a requested number of features during training by learning which inputs to preserve and which to replace with Gaussian noise.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning can extract useful representations from single-cell measurements, but a method's value depends on the analysis those representations support. scSSL-Bench evaluates nineteen methods across nine datasets. It covers batch correction, cell type annotation, and missing modality prediction, and systematically compares the data augmentation strategies used during learning.

The results reveal task-dependent strengths. Specialized single-cell methods, including scVI, CLAIRE, and fine-tuned scGPT, perform particularly well at batch correction with one modality. Generic self-supervised methods such as VICReg and SimCLR perform better at cell typing and multimodal integration. These findings make the downstream task central to choosing a representation-learning method.

Across the evaluated tasks, random masking is the most effective augmentation strategy, outperforming domain-specific alternatives. The authors also identify a need for a specialized framework for multimodal single-cell integration. The benchmark supplies a common evaluation platform and concrete guidance grounded in these comparisons. Its recommendations reflect measured trade-offs across the tested tasks, rather than identifying one method as the best choice for every single-cell analysis.
icml-2025-scssl-bench-benchmarking-self-.tldr: scSSL-Bench compares nineteen methods and finds task-specific winners, with random masking the strongest augmentation across its evaluated single-cell tasks.

paragraphs: Safety-related behavior in language models can be studied through directions in their internal activation space. Earlier work represented refusal with a single direction. This paper examines representation changes during safety fine-tuning of Llama 3 8B for refusing jailbreaks and finds a multidimensional structure underlying the resulting safety-aligned behavior.

By analyzing orthogonal directions, the authors identify a dominant direction governing refusal and several smaller directions associated with interpretable features, including hypothetical narratives and role-playing. They then measure how these secondary directions promote or suppress the dominant one. This shows that refusal behavior depends on interactions among multiple representational features in the studied model.

The authors also demonstrate that removing certain trigger tokens from harmful queries can weaken these directions and bypass the learned safety behavior. This finding links the internal representation analysis to an observed vulnerability. The contribution is a more detailed mechanistic account of alignment in this setting: secondary features can shape refusal even when one direction appears to dominate the overall behavior.
icml-2025-the-hidden-dimensions-of-llm-a.tldr: An analysis of safety-tuned Llama 3 8B finds that multiple interacting activation directions shape refusal and help explain alignment vulnerabilities.

paragraphs: Supervised fine-tuning datasets can contain useful examples whose individual tokens vary in relevance. Even a high-quality sample may include phrases that add little task information after pretraining, and continued training on them can hurt downstream performance. This paper therefore studies data selection at the token level rather than only at the example level.

The proposed pipeline treats token quality through a noisy-label perspective. It estimates quality by examining how model updates influence each token, then applies a threshold to separate informative tokens from uninformative ones. The influence measurement can use one pass with a fixed reference model or an iterative process with reference models that evolve.

The authors analyze the benefits and limitations of both variants using theoretical error upper bounds. Extensive experiments show consistent downstream improvements from the framework. The contribution is a finer-grained way to direct fine-tuning toward task-specific information: useful content can be retained even when other tokens in the same sample contribute little or potentially interfere with learning.
icml-2025-token-cleaning-fine-grained-da.tldr: Token Cleaning improves supervised fine-tuning by using update-based influence estimates to filter uninformative tokens within training examples.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks learn from relations between entities, but many systems also contain interactions involving several entities together. Topological deep learning models these higher-order structures. Combinatorial Complex Neural Networks provide an expressive approach, yet the lack of standardized development frameworks makes such models harder to build and apply.

The paper introduces Generalized Combinatorial Complex Neural Networks, or GCCNs, as a systematic way to transform neural networks, including graph networks, into topological counterparts. The authors prove that GCCNs generalize and subsume existing CCNNs. This establishes a model family that includes the earlier framework while supporting a broader range of architectures.

Experiments across diverse GCCNs show that they consistently match or outperform CCNNs, often with lower model complexity. TopoTune supplies lightweight software for defining, building, and training these models flexibly. The contribution combines a formal extension of the architecture family with practical development support, making higher-order modeling more accessible while retaining the performance benefits demonstrated in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-topotune-a-framework-for-gener.tldr: TopoTune supports a generalized family of topological neural networks that subsumes CCNNs and often matches or improves their performance with less complexity.

paragraphs: Software engineering agents need environments where they can work on code and receive meaningful feedback. SWE-Gym provides 2,438 real-world Python tasks, each containing a codebase, an executable runtime, unit tests, and a natural-language task description. These elements create concrete training situations in which an agent's proposed changes can be exercised.

The authors use this environment to train language-model-based agents, reporting gains of up to 19 percentage points in resolve rate on SWE-Bench Verified and Lite. They also train verifiers using agent trajectories sampled from SWE-Gym and investigate inference-time scaling. This extends the use of the environment from training agents to training systems that assess their work.

Combining the fine-tuned agents with the verifier approach yields resolve rates of 32.0% on Verified and 26.0% on Lite, reported as a new state of the art for open-weight software engineering agents. The release includes the environment, models, and trajectories. Together, these resources support further work on both agent training and verification using executable software tasks.
icml-2025-training-software-engineering-.tldr: SWE-Gym supplies executable Python tasks for training software agents and verifiers, producing substantial resolve-rate gains on SWE-Bench.

paragraphs: High-dimensional Bayesian optimization has a reputation for being difficult, yet recent work found that simple methods can perform well on real-world tasks. This paper investigates that apparent contradiction. It examines which parts of the optimization process cause failures and which design choices help explain the success of comparatively simple approaches.

The empirical analysis identifies vanishing gradients caused by Gaussian-process initialization schemes as a major contributor to failure. It also finds that methods encouraging local search are better suited to the task. Maximum likelihood estimation of Gaussian-process length scales proves sufficient for state-of-the-art performance in the study, making the way these parameters are fitted especially consequential.

Building on these findings, the authors propose MSR, a simple variant of maximum likelihood estimation, and report state-of-the-art performance across a comprehensive set of real-world applications. Targeted experiments illustrate and confirm their explanations. The results identify specific, addressable causes of poor performance and show that effective high-dimensional optimization can arise from careful choices within a relatively simple modeling approach.
icml-2025-understanding-high-dimensional.tldr: The paper links high-dimensional Bayesian optimization failures to initialization-induced vanishing gradients and develops a successful simple maximum-likelihood variant.

paragraphs: Mechanistic interpretability tries to explain a neural network's computation through its internal components. Yet an explanation needs criteria for what it means to capture that computation. This paper addresses the often informal status of mechanistic interpretations by proposing explicit axioms for the relationship between a network and its interpretation.

The framework draws inspiration from abstract interpretation in program analysis, where approximate descriptions are used to represent program semantics. Here, a mechanistic interpretation must approximately capture the network's semantics in a compositional way. The emphasis on composition means that descriptions of internal parts must fit together into an account of the computation being analyzed.

The authors demonstrate the axioms on an existing, well-known interpretability study and on a new case involving a Transformer trained to solve 2-SAT. These cases illustrate how the formal criteria can validate proposed interpretations. The contribution is a principled basis for assessing explanations, with approximation built into the definition, rather than requiring an interpretation to reproduce every detail of the network.
icml-2025-validating-mechanistic-interpr.tldr: The paper proposes axioms for validating mechanistic explanations as compositional approximations of a neural network's computation.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate high-quality samples, but directing them toward a particular objective often requires extra training or a guidance method tailored to one task. This paper revisits guidance through variational inference and control. Its goal is to steer the trajectory of a pretrained diffusion model according to a cost on the final output.

The proposed framework, Diffusion Trajectory Matching, brings a broad class of guidance methods into a common formulation and supports new methods within it. The terminal cost expresses what the completed generation should satisfy. Framing guidance around the trajectory connects changes made during generation to that final objective, providing a shared basis for designing guidance procedures.

The authors introduce one such procedure and report state-of-the-art results on several linear, nonlinear, and blind inverse problems. It requires no additional model training and is not specific to either pixel-space or latent-space diffusion models. The contribution therefore includes both a unifying perspective on guidance and an instantiated method with strong results across the evaluated inverse-problem settings.
icml-2025-variational-control-for-guidan.tldr: Diffusion Trajectory Matching unifies guidance through variational control and yields a training-free method with strong inverse-problem results.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains policies from fixed datasets, avoiding the costs and risks of extensive real-world exploration. However, the recorded behavior may be suboptimal, and the lack of interaction can make value estimates inaccurate. VeoRL investigates whether diverse unlabeled videos available online can provide additional knowledge useful for learning control.

The method constructs an interactive world model from this video data and uses model-based behavior guidance to support the agent in its target domain. Its purpose is to transfer knowledge about physical dynamics and control behavior from natural videos. The world model supplies a route for applying that information within the offline learning process.

Experiments cover visual control in robotic manipulation, autonomous driving, and open-world video games. VeoRL reports substantial performance improvements, exceeding 100% in some cases. That qualification matters: the largest gains are specific reported cases, not a uniform improvement across every task. The results support using broad video data as a source of behavioral and physical knowledge for model-based offline reinforcement learning.
icml-2025-video-enhanced-offline-reinfor.tldr: VeoRL builds an interactive world model from unlabeled videos to guide offline reinforcement learning, achieving substantial gains across several visual-control domains.
